newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Euro markets tremble after Wall St tumble.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Euro markets tremble after Wall St tumble.

text.p: European stock and bond markets faced a stern test on Monday after Wall Street tumbled 2.27 percent on Friday and U.S. Treasuries slid lower.
Stock markets throughout Europe opened sharply lower, stung by the 148 point fall in the Dow Jones Industrials Average and wary of important U.S. data and earnings figures due this week.

The foreign exchange market was cautious, too, although comments by Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka that Japan would act decisively against excessive currency movements failed to have much impact on the dollar in Europe.
Bond markets in Europe, like equity markets, started the week under pressure with investor focus fixed firmly on the United States.

With the Dow industrials nearly 10 percent off their record highs, options expirations pending and the yield on the 30-year Treasury bond nearing the key 7.25 percent level, U.S. analysts said volatility was all but guaranteed.
The first major test will come on Tuesday when the U.S. government will report March retail inflation.

Although economic data have so far shown robust growth and subdued inflation, a stronger than expected consumer inflation figure after Friday's producer price index rise could be a major confirmation of impending price pressures.
Many market watchers already expect another rise in U.S. interest rates when the Federal Reserve's policy-making open market committee meets next month, and rising prices would underline the threat.

A slew of first-quarter earnings reports by U.S. companies, such as Intel Microsoft and General Motors, will also weigh heavily on investors contemplating the prospect that Dow may still have another five percent to fall.
Wall Street's Friday tumble had an immediate impact on the major European markets, with the blue chip indices in both Paris and Frankfurt being marked down more than two percent at the start.
London fell sharply, too, but it recouped more than half its losses by mid-morning and traders said they were waiting to see which way Wall Street would jump later.
"Some people are still hoping that the FTSE will decouple from the Dow. But if the Dow keeps sliding, we will go with it," ane London dealer said.
"It's only a question of degree. We won't match it point for point but there is no way we can avoid catching a pretty big cold."
By 0915 GMT the FTSE 100 index was showing losses of ... having gained some support from figures showing British producer prices fell 0.1 percent in March.
German shares fell heavily at the start of bourse trade, mirroring the slide in pre-bourse dealings.
Dealers said the strong dollar and steady government bonds were lending some support but attention was on the Dow.
"We are all looking to see how much Wall Street can salvage from (Friday's) wreckage later on -- that will be the determining factor," said one Frankfurt-based equity salesman.
The DAX-30 index of leading German shares was down 1.8 percent by late morning, with software group SAP among the sharpest losers, down 11.40 marks at 274.6.
The story was much the same in Paris where the CAC-40 index tumbled more than two percent at the start but recouped about half its losses later.
The blue-chip index, which lost 1.28 percent on Friday, was standing 1.12 percent down at 2,545.84 points by 0915 GMT after bouncing off a low of 2,528.30 points.
"The market's looking pretty resilient. Wall Street was down, but the dollar is looking very solid," a trader said.
SGS-Thomson underperformed, falling 4.15 percent to 376.5 francs after reporting a drop in first-quarter net income to $90.50 million from $175 million.
The dollar was holding steady above 1.72 marks and around 126.5 yen with dealers reporting the tone firm but cautious ahead of Wall Street reopening.
"There is some nervousness to the dollar if the Dow takes another hit this week," said Lee Ferridge, currency strategist at Commerzbank in London. "But if it steadies, the dollar could really fly."
Comments by the Japanese finance minister failed to dent the currency, particularly after he denied he had set a specific intervention level around 127 to 128 yen.

"Unless the Ministry of Finance and Bank of Japan renounce their recent pledge to keep monetary policy accommodative, intervention would have only the momentary effect of shaking out some of the short-term speculative players," said Ken Landon, analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Tokyo.
CURRENCIES AT 0915 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 1.7226 marks and 126.44 yen compared with 1.7255 marks and 126.15 yen in late European trading on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 0915 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was down 21.5 points, or 0.5 percent, at 4,249.2.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was 28.72 points, or 1.12 percent, at 2,545.84.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was 60.22 points, or 1.8 percent, at 3,279.83.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold fixed lower at $346.65 from Friday's $347.95. Silver was quoted five cents lower at $4.74.
